chapter_theme: The sea-bathing chapter: a vidyadhara and his beloved fly from the silver mountain to Puhar's Indra festival, where he explains its guardian bhuta and halls as Indra's gifts to a Chola, traces Madhavi's line to a celestial dancer cursed to earth and names the eleven dances of the gods she performs; after the festival Madhavi adorns herself, gives the sulking Kovalan union and sulk, and at the full moon they ride at dawn through Puhar's streets and lamp-lit market to the crowded shore, where she sits with him in a bower and takes up the lute.

cast.role: a vidyadhara (sky-dwelling being) of the silver mountain who visits Puhar's festival
the vidyadhara's beloved, to whom he speaks
the dancer of Puhar of the celestial dancer's line, Kovalan's lover
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, living with Madhavi
the auspicious women who scatter flowers, grass and paddy before the couple

silappathikaram:6:1-17.reading: A vidyadhara warrior, holding a love-feast with his long-eyed beloved in a grove on the slopes of the silver mountain, tells her that this is the day a rich city in the south begins its festival for Indra, and proposes that they go to see the place where the great bhuta sits and eats offerings, the bhuta the king of the gods sent to the lance-bearing king who guarded the royal city against the asuras and turned back their deceit, and the order of the five assembly-halls that king won from the immortal for guarding Amaravati and set upon earth.
silappathikaram:6:1-17.nuance: Puhar is not named: it enters the epic's second festival chapter as 'a rich city in the south' seen from a heavenly being's distance, and what he wants to see first are its sacred fixtures, which the unit explains as heaven's rewards to a Chola who once guarded Indra's own city. The festival is thus framed as a debt between the gods and the Chola line. The king is named only by epithets (தொடுகழல் மன்னன், திருந்துவேல் அண்ணல்).
silappathikaram:6:1-17.event: A vidyadhara feasting with his beloved on the silver mountain proposes that they fly south to see the Indra festival of Puhar.

silappathikaram:6:18-26.reading: He goes on: they will hear the song that knows the beauty of Narada's lute and the refrain sung by the leading singer, and see the dance of the snake-hipped girl born in the line of the maiden Madhavi, who, when Urvasi failed in her dance before the thousand-eyed Indra and the music lost its auspiciousness, was cursed to stay on earth with the lute; and he ends by hailing his coral-lipped, drum-waisted beloved.
silappathikaram:6:18-26.nuance: The syntax of lines 20 to 24 is hard to fix: the one cursed is called மங்கை மாதவி, and whether that is Urvasi herself under another name or a second celestial dancer is not settled by the lines. What is clear is that the earthly Madhavi's art is presented as an inheritance from a heavenly dancer's fall: her dancing on earth is the continuation of a curse. Line 26 closes the vidyadhara's speech with a vocative.
silappathikaram:6:18-26.unit_note: Boundary moved: the source unit 18-29 ran on into the next sentence; the vidyadhara's first speech closes at line 26 with the vocative துடிஇடை யோயே, and line 27 begins the narration of his journey, so the unit now ends at 26 and the next begins at 27.

silappathikaram:6:27-45.reading: Saying they will worship the lord of the immortals, he shows his beloved the Himalaya, the Ganga, Ujjain, the Vindhya forest, the Venkatam hill and the Kaveri country, reaches Puhar, worships there in due order, sings the songs to Mayon, to the bhutas of the four varnas and to the moon, and then begins to point out the dances: the kodukotti that Siva, with Uma as one half of him, danced when the three cities burned at the gods' request and the fiery arrow obeyed, and the pandarangam he danced with the four-faced Brahma watching from before the chariot.
silappathikaram:6:27-45.nuance: The flight runs north to south across the whole subcontinent and ends at the Kaveri, so Puhar's festival is set at the end of a sacred geography. The dances are told as myths of origin: each stage form is what a god once danced at a victory, and the Tripura burning is given as a literal event (the gods asked, the arrow obeyed). பாரதி ஆடிய பாரதி அரங்கத்து (line 39) names Siva and his stage by a title whose sense the lines do not fix.
silappathikaram:6:27-45.unit_note: Boundary moved: begins at line 27 (formerly inside unit 18-29), where the narration of the journey starts after the speech that ends at line 26; it ends at 45 as before.
silappathikaram:6:27-45.event: The vidyadhara flies with his beloved over the northern mountains and rivers to Puhar, worships Indra, sings, and begins to name the dances.

silappathikaram:6:46-67.reading: The vidyadhara names the rest of the eleven dances, each a god's dance at a victory: Krishna's alliyam against Kamsa's deceit and his wrestling dance, Murugan's drum dance on the sea's wave-stage after overcoming Sur and his umbrella dance before the disarmed asuras, the pot dance of the one who measured the earth in Bana's city, Kama's dance in a woman's guise, Durga's stilt dance, Lakshmi's doll dance and Indrani's kadaiyam at the northern gate, and bids his beloved see them performed with each one's costume, stances and songs in strict rule.
silappathikaram:6:46-67.nuance: Almost every dance is the celebration of a god overcoming an asura or a deceit (வஞ்சம்), and the gods are drawn from every cult (Siva, Krishna, Murugan, Kama, Durga, Lakshmi, Indrani) under one festival for Indra. Lines 66 and 67 repeat almost word for word the formula of Madhavi's training in the third kaathai (பதினோர் ஆடலும் ... விதிமாண் கொள்கையின் விளங்க), so the dances learned there are here performed.
silappathikaram:6:46-67.event: The vidyadhara points out to his beloved the eleven dances of the gods as they are performed at the festival.

silappathikaram:6:68-83.reading: Having told his beloved that this is Madhavi of the line of the Madhavi he spoke of in the grove, the vidyadhara rejoices; and when the festival that the sky-dwellers come to watch unseen, and its dances, costumes and ornaments have ended, Madhavi, to please the man who sat sulking, washes her fragrant hair in water steeped with ten astringents, five scents and thirty-two herbs, dries it in smoke, works musk paste into it, and colours her small feet with lac.
silappathikaram:6:68-83.nuance: The unit turns from heaven to the bedroom in one sentence: the heavenly watcher's recognition (மாதவி மரபின் மாதவி இவள்) is the last of the celestial frame, and the next person seen is a man sulking after the festival. Why Kovalan sulks the text does not say; that it follows her public dancing is a reader's inference. The man in ஊடல் கோலம் is unnamed here and is Kovalan by line 109.
silappathikaram:6:68-83.event: The vidyadhara identifies Madhavi to his beloved; after the festival Madhavi bathes and perfumes her hair and paints her feet to please the sulking Kovalan.

silappathikaram:6:84-98.reading: Madhavi puts five kinds of anklet on her feet, a ring on her thigh, a girdle of thirty-two strands of pearl over fine cloth, armlets of pure gems, bangles of gold, conch and coral on her forearms, and rings shaped like a fish's mouth, of red gems and of diamond and emerald on her soft fingers.
silappathikaram:6:84-98.nuance: The catalogue is the poem's own display of wealth worn on a body, moving from foot to finger; among its first items are anklets of five names (பரியகம் நூபுரம் பாடகம் சதங்கை அரியகம்), in a story whose turn will rest on one anklet.
silappathikaram:6:84-98.event: Madhavi adorns her feet, thighs, waist, arms and fingers with anklets, girdle, armlets, bangles and rings.

silappathikaram:6:99-114.reading: She puts fine chains and a necklace on her throat, a string of gems to hide the small of her back, ear-ornaments of sapphire and moonstone and the god's crest, the conch and other jewels on her dark hair; and she who had given Kovalan both union and sulking and sat on the couch fit for song, when the full moon came to the old city and crowds streamed toward the sea, longed to see the sea-play on the flowering shore and asked for it.
silappathikaram:6:99-114.nuance: Line 109 makes union and sulking things Madhavi gives (அளித்து) to Kovalan: the woman dispenses both sides of love's play, and the one who sulked was he (line 75). The wish to see the sea-play is hers, so the outing that will part them starts from her desire.
silappathikaram:6:99-114.event: Adorned, Madhavi, having given Kovalan union and sulking, asks to go to see the full-moon sea bathing on the shore.

silappathikaram:6:115-132.reading: At dawn, when the birds of the lotus pond cry, the cock announces the watch and the morning star clears the dark, Kovalan of the rain-like giving hand mounts a mule and deer-eyed Madhavi a carriage, and they pass the street of piled wealth and the altar street where auspicious women carrying lamps scatter flowers, grass and paddy with jingling ornaments, go straight past the seat of the goddess of fortune and down the city's middle street, toward the quarter where foreign merchants raise flags on the sea sand.
silappathikaram:6:115-132.nuance: Kovalan is named here by his liberality (வான வண்கையன், the man whose hand gives like the sky), and the couple's road runs through the heaped wealth and 'the seat of Tirumagal' (line 127); a reader who knows that his wealth will be gone by the ninth kaathai may hear the passage as a farewell to fortune, but that is interpretation, not the text's statement.
silappathikaram:6:115-132.event: At dawn Kovalan rides a mule and Madhavi a carriage through Puhar's rich streets, greeted by auspicious women with lamps, flowers, grass and paddy.

silappathikaram:6:133-149.reading: They reach the evening quarter by the market, where the lamps of every trade shine together beyond counting, those of sellers of colours, sandal, flowers, powders and goods, of skilled craftsmen, of sweet-makers and pancake-sellers, of women hawkers and fish-sellers, the lighthouse on the shore, the lamps of the net-fishers' boats, of foreign-tongued strangers and of the watchmen of cargo, and beside them the lotus waters and the bounds of the farmland appear.
silappathikaram:6:133-149.nuance: The lamps are counted by trade, so the catalogue is a census of the port: each light belongs to a livelihood, from the hawker woman to the lighthouse and the foreigners whose speech is strange (பொழிபெயர் தேஎத்தர்). Lines 145 to 147 (the sand like pounded flour, கடிப்பகை காணும் காட்சியது) are obscure and the reading of them is a guess.
silappathikaram:6:133-149.event: Kovalan and Madhavi pass through the market and shore of Puhar lit by the lamps of every trade.

silappathikaram:6:150-174.reading: On the neythal shore hedged with thazhai, where ships unload the goods of hill and sea and princes, merchants' sons, dancing and singing women and many companies gather behind screens, with different costumes and noises, like the first day of Karikal Valavan's festival of the cool water, and the clamour of the four varnas fills the Kaveri's mouth, Madhavi of long flower-eyes sits with Kovalan on a canopied couch under a punnai inside a thazhai fence, taking the tuned lute from Vasanthamaalai.
silappathikaram:6:150-174.nuance: The crowd is compared to Karikal Valavan's festival with the phrase தண்பதம் கொள்ளும் தலைநாள், the same words (தண்பதம் கொண்டு) that Akananuru 376 uses for Karikal's water festival at Kazhar: the epic recalls the Sangam king as a past glory, not as the ruling Chola. The unit closes with the lute passing into Madhavi's hand, the instrument of the songs in the next kaathai that will part the lovers.
silappathikaram:6:150-174.event: On the crowded Puhar shore Madhavi sits with Kovalan in a screened bower under a punnai and takes the lute from Vasanthamaalai.

silappathikaram:6:175-178.reading: A closing venba says that the jewel-like bee that slept at evening inside the white petal of the seaside thazhai went at morning to suck the pollen of the honeyed flower, and the beautiful bright sun's chariot appeared.
silappathikaram:6:175-178.nuance: On its face a dawn scene; read against the story it may picture Kovalan, the bee who spent the night in one flower and leaves it at morning for another, which the next kaathai makes real. That second sense is an interpretation; நறவம் may be honey or the name of a flower.

links.note: The fifth kaathai shows Puhar's warriors and women making offerings at the guardian bhuta's altar that Indra sent; here the vidyadhara tells why it was sent: a Chola guarded Amaravati against the asuras and received the bhuta and the five halls as Indra's gift.
links.teaches: Read together, the townspeople's worship and the outsider's origin story show the festival as heaven repaying a Chola's service, which the city's own rite does not explain.

links.note: The third kaathai says a sage's curse on Indra's son and a celestial woman was lifted at the dance stage, and introduces Madhavi; here a celestial dancer is cursed to earth for failing before Indra, and Madhavi is of her line.
links.teaches: Madhavi's art is given a heavenly genealogy rooted in a fall: the courtesan's dancing on earth is the continuation of a curse that her first performance was said to end.

links.note: Lines 66-67 repeat the formula of Madhavi's training (பதினோர் ஆடலும் ... விதிமாண் கொள்கையின் விளங்க) from the third kaathai, now as the dances a heavenly watcher sees her perform.
links.teaches: The repeated formula marks what was learned as a girl's curriculum turning into a public festival performance watched even by beings of the sky.

links.note: The epic tells Siva's burning of the three cities as an event (the gods asked, the fiery arrow obeyed) and the origin of a dance staged at a city festival; Tirumular calls those who say Siva burned the three cities fools and makes the cities the three impurities.
links.teaches: The same myth stands in one text as a literal victory reenacted by a courtesan for a crowd and in the other as an inner allegory whose literal telling is folly; the conflict depends on reading the epic's account as a statement of event.

gains.a: the epic's festival myth is shown to be one available reading, the literal and performative one, which a Saiva yogic text explicitly rejects
gains.b: Tirumular's 'fools' get a concrete target: a public culture in which the Tripura burning was danced on a stage as history

links.note: The couplet's man says sulking is love's sweetness and the embrace after it sulking's sweetness; the epic says Madhavi gave Kovalan both union and sulking, after he had sat in a sulk.
links.teaches: In the epic the two halves of the couplet's cycle are things a trained woman gives, so ūdal becomes an art supplied to a lover rather than only a mood that lovers fall into.

gains.a: Madhavi's giving of ஊடல் and கூடல் is placed in the Kural's account of love, where sulking followed by union is love's fullest pleasure
gains.b: the couplet's private cycle is shown inside a courtesan's house, where it can be practised and offered, which raises the question the couplet does not ask, whose feeling it is

links.note: The quatrain says the harlot's love is like a lamp that dies when its oil is spent; here Madhavi, a courtesan, gives Kovalan union and sulking and herself asks for the outing, and in the story it is Kovalan, not she, who breaks off (silappathikaram:7:286-300).
links.teaches: The epic's courtesan breaks the quatrain's rule from the other side: the love ends, but by the man's suspicion on the shore, not by her turning away when his wealth runs out.

gains.a: Madhavi's devotion in this unit is set against the moral literature's verdict on her class, which makes it pointed rather than merely decorative
gains.b: the quatrain's general rule meets a counter-case in the classical story most read by Tamil readers, which limits it to a type rather than every courtesan

links.note: The Pattinappalai's fishermen count the coloured lights of Puhar's mansions at night; the epic counts the shore's lamps by trade, from perfume-sellers and hawkers to the lighthouse, fishing boats and foreign traders.
links.teaches: The idyll's lights are a spectacle watched from the boats, while the epic's are a roll of the port's livelihoods, showing how the later poem turns the same harbour of lights into a social survey.

gains.a: the epic's catalogue gains a Sangam precedent for Puhar as a city known by its lights, which marks it as a set piece of the port, not a passing detail
gains.b: the idyll's anonymous lights gain owners: the epic names who keeps each lamp, filling in the trades behind the glow

links.note: Both use the phrase of Karikal 'taking the cool water' (தண்பதம் கொள்ளும் / தண்பதம் கொண்டு): in the Akananuru a courtesan recalls how at Karikal's water festival at Kazhar the Kaveri carried off the dancer Atthi, and likens her lover's loss to it; the epic likens the joyful crowd on the shore to the first day of that festival.
links.teaches: The festival the epic uses as a simile of joy is, in the Sangam poem, the scene of a dancer lost and a courtesan abandoned, which is what this shore day will become for Madhavi.

gains.a: the simile carries a buried memory of loss at the same festival, so the epic's joyful shore is shadowed before the songs begin
gains.b: the Akananuru's water festival gains a fuller picture of its crowds, costumes and noise and of its standing as a byword for Puhar's festivity

links.note: The Pattinappalai's speaker, in the poem for Karikal, swears he will not leave his long-haired woman even if given all of Puhar; the epic, invoking Karikal's festival, seats Kovalan beside Madhavi on Puhar's shore, where before evening he will leave her (silappathikaram:7:286-300).
links.teaches: The idyll's vow that no city outweighs the beloved is tested on the very shore it praised, and the epic's lover fails it amid Puhar's full splendour.

gains.a: Kovalan's coming desertion is measured against a famous Sangam refusal to leave a woman for Puhar, which sharpens its cost
gains.b: the idyll's hyperbole gains a narrative counter-case showing that leaving was the choice it imagined refusing

links.note: Here the lute passes into Madhavi's hand in a bower set up for pleasure; in the next kaathai the songs she sings on it make Kovalan think her false, and, his ūzhvinai coming to fruit, he leaves her on the shore.
links.teaches: The instrument and the place prepared for the lovers' pleasure become the means and site of their parting, which the next kaathai assigns to karma acting through the lute's music.

new_concepts.gloss: the festival of a town or shrine, with its crowds, music, dance, offerings and feasting
new_concepts.label_source: text: இந்திர விழவு line 6, மகிழ்விழா line 34, வானவன் விழவு line 73

new_concepts.gloss: a curse that binds its object to a fate, often a fall into earthly birth

source_issues: The kaathai header says the text has 178 lines but its printed last line number is 170; the akaval runs to line 174 here and the closing venba is 175-178, so the edition's own numbering and this count differ.
Lines 73 and 111 carry a repaired TSCII leftover (a ு plus a following letter read as ூ), flagged by show; the repaired lines read sensibly.
Lines 145-147 (இடிக்கலப்பு அன்ன ஈர்அயில் மருங்கில் கடிப்பகை காணும் காட்சியது ஆகிய) are obscure and their reading is uncertain.
Lines 20-24: the syntax leaves unclear whether the cursed மங்கை மாதவி is Urvasi or another celestial dancer.
